narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated a 52.7% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is only slightly above a coin flip, so this is not a certainty, but it was enough for the model to classify you as more likely than not to fail.

The strongest factor driving that prediction was your LSAT score. Your score of 28.50 is well below the average of 37.18 among accepted students, and it was the single largest influence pushing the prediction toward bar-exam failure. The next most important factor was your undergraduate GPA. Your 3.40 is above the accepted-student average of 3.23, so this worked in your favor and pushed toward passing. The third most important factor was your first-year class decile. Your value of 5, compared with an accepted average of 6, also contributed toward passing, though less strongly.

Because your LSAT was the clearest risk signal, your next step should be to focus on improving it—retaking the LSAT after structured preparation and aiming for a score closer to the accepted average. You should also speak with admissions about whether an appeal, conditional admission, or feedback appointment is available, and consider strengthening your application with additional academic evidence or a later reapplication once your profile is stronger.
